newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Bonn seeks more active role in Cyprus problem.
newsitem.headline: Bonn seeks more active role in Cyprus problem.

text.p: Germany is seeking a more active role to help resolve the Cyprus dispute ahead of the island's entry talks with the European Union, a German official said on Monday.

"We do not see ourselves in the role of an independent mediator," said Detlev Rantzau. "What we shall be trying to do is to try and support anything and everything that the United Nations are doing to find a solution to the conflict."

Rantzau, a career diplomat, has spent the past five days on a fact-finding mission on the divided eastern Mediterranean island, a main source of tension between NATO partners Greece and Turkey. He was recently appointed Bonn's special representative on the Cyprus question.
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since a Turkish invasion in 1974 sparked by a Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Greece.

Rantzau is the latest in a small army of mediators to have grappled with the Cyprus dispute. United Nations attempts spanning decades to reunite the island as a bicommunal federation of Greek and Turkish Cypriots have led nowhere.
A solution to the problem has taken on added urgency ahead of entry talks the internationally recognised Greek Cypriot-led government is due to start with the European Union in 1998.
The breakaway Turkish Cypriot administration in northern Cyprus declared in 1983 is recognised only by Ankara which has some 30,000 troops stationed there.

The EU element, the renewal of tension between Greece and Turkey and the possible effects that could have on Cyprus spurred German involvement, Rantzau said, speaking at a bullet-riddled hotel used by British peacekeepers as living quarters in the U.N.-controlled buffer zone splitting through the capital Nicosia.

"My government thought that as a member of the European Union and as a member of NATO we should manifest our renewed engagement in trying to help in finding a solution to the problem by appointing a special envoy for the Cyprus question."

The U.N. mission on the island has been holding proximity talks between the two sides since March to prepare for direct talks between the leaders of the two communities by the end of June. If the meeting takes place it will be the first between the two leaders in almost three years.
"I think whatever the differences and opinions the only way to come to a solution is to start discussing them," Rantzau said.
